extracted.intended_audience: Coq users/contributors writing and maintaining Coq source files and proof scripts (Rocq community)
extracted.subtask_description: Style and best-practice guidelines for writing legible, reusable Coq source files and proof scripts, as collected on the Rocq wiki. Covers file structure, comment conventions, proof layout, naming, variable naming, and extraction hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: File header / copyright and license block
rubrics_metrics.description:
Following the shape of the files in the standard library of Coq, start the Coq files with a comment of the form
( *
**********************************************************************
*)
( *
Copyright <YEAR> <AUTHOR>
*)
( *
<LICENSE>
*)
( *
**********************************************************************
*)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This will credit the author(s) and clarifies any license issues, which is necessary for re-usability of your code. Include this header at the top of the file to make reuse and attribution explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coqdoc-style comments for structure (but not inside proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use coqdoc-style comments graciously, to clarify the structure of your formalisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, try not to use them inside proofs. Instead use ordinary (*  *) comments. This is because proofs are less likely to be processed via coqdoc and usually they are suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent use of blank lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use blank lines consistently (I.e. use the same number of blank lines between all lemmas in a section).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent blank-line usage improves legibility. Also: end the file with a newline character.

rubrics_metrics.name: End file with newline
rubrics_metrics.description: End the file with a newline character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A final newline is a small but standard requirement for many tooling and version-control conventions; include it for neatness and compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start proofs with a line containing "Proof."
rubrics_metrics.description:
Start the proofs using a line containing
Proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having a dedicated line beginning the proof makes proofs easier to scan and parse by humans and tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation for multiple subgoals
rubrics_metrics.description: When a tactic generates more than one subgoal use indentation for tactics that are used for solving each subgoal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example layout given where you label/comment each subgoal and indent the body for each (e.g., after case (compare_with_zero X) put a comment for each branch and indent the tactics that solve that branch). Indentation clarifies which tactics belong to which subgoal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment complicated/lengthy subgoal segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use comments when using complicated or lengthy proof segments on subgoals of case, induction, destruct and their friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add explanatory comments for complex segments to help future readers and maintainers understand the strategy applied to each subgoal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use blank lines to separate proof segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use blank lines to separate different segments of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group proof steps into logical segments (e.g., setup, main argument, cleanup) separated by blank lines to improve readability and navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative layout: indentation indicating remaining subgoals
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternate possible layout is to use indentation to tell exactly how many subgoals remain: n indentation for n subgoals (variant: (n-1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is especially useful during development when you replay proofs after you have modified a definition above: you can easily find where your proof script behaves differently. It fits better with a forward proof-style using assert-like tactics, though the document notes it can look less nice than the labeled-branch style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform naming convention for inductive types and related items
rubrics_metrics.description: It is good practice to use a uniform naming convention for inductive data-types, their constructors, the inverse of the constructors (provable by inversion) and the strong elimination rules (generated by Scheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep naming patterns consistent across a development so constructors, inverses, and elimination principles are recognizable and predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform naming for lemmas; follow standard library when in doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: For lemmas try to follow a uniform naming convention based on the subject of the formalisation. If in doubt use the naming pattern used for similar lemmas that is used in the Coq standard library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting names analogous to the standard library eases discoverability and makes your development feel familiar to Coq users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly name hypotheses introduced in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usually a good idea to explicitly give names to all the hypothesis that are introduced by Coq. This makes reuse of the code easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intros to name assumptions explicitly. For destruct, induction and similar tactics, use the as keyword to give explicit names. Conversely, use underscore (_) to clear variables that are not useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraction: use proper Haskell module naming and extract whole generated code
rubrics_metrics.description: When extracting to Haskell, note that Haskell module names should start with an upper-case letter. It is best practice to use the whole Coq generated code as a Haskell module and write your own pretty printing interface for it (in fact this is the default behaviour of the extraction mechanism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Instead of simply capitalising the first letter, the page suggests using e.g.:
Extraction Language Haskell.
Extraction "Xfoo.hs" foo.
to extract a Coq constant foo into Haskell module Xfoo.hs. This emphasises that the Haskell file is a result of Coq extraction and avoids ad-hoc renaming of pieces.
